Out to the edge of the universe we can see

Past the Local Group and a quasar to the oldest light. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Out to the edge of the universe we can see

We start at home

Our galaxy is about 87 000 light-years across, with between one and four hundred billion stars. Seen from outside, as here, it is a model: nobody has ever left it to look back.

Our group of galaxies

Six million light-years out, our galaxy and Andromeda are the two large members of a group of more than a hundred galaxies, most of them small. Where each one is has been measured; the shapes of the big spirals are models.

The local volume

Forty million light-years out, our group is one knot among eight hundred galaxies. Most of their distances have been measured. The fainter grey-blue points are only estimates: their direction is known, their depth is not.

TON 618, a quasar

TON 618 is a quasar: gas blazing as it falls into a black hole of about forty billion Suns. Its light left 10.8 billion years ago. Space has stretched since, so the map draws it where our model of the universe puts it now: about 18 billion light-years away.

Where the first galaxies are now

The James Webb telescope has seen galaxies whose light left when the universe was about three hundred million years old. Those galaxies are now about 34 billion light-years away, in a few small patches of our sky. None is drawn on this map.

The microwave background

This is the oldest light there is, released about 370 000 years after the Big Bang. The map is measured: a NASA spacecraft charted it across our whole sky. Painting it on this sphere, where the light set out, is an illustration; seen from anywhere else, it would differ.

The end of this map

Nearly fifty billion light-years out, this map ends. What we can see ends sooner, about 46 billion light-years away: farther light has not had time to reach us. Nothing measured lies past it, so this band is an illustration. Space goes on; our view of it does not.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
